# Irritants and asphyxiants

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Toxicologic disorders > Irritants and asphyxiants*

[Original Article Link](/library/_Q05Af)

---

## Summary

Exposure to <u>chemical asphyxiants</u> and/or irritants can occur in the household or workplace, in the context of war or terror attacks, or as a result of natural or man-made disasters. Irritants such as <u>ammonia</u>, <u>chlorine</u>, <u>phosgene</u>, and <u>tear gas</u> are chemical agents that cause irritation or an inflammatory <u>skin</u> and <u>mucous membrane</u> response. Exposure to irritants can lead to <u>cough</u>, <u>eye</u> irritation, <u>mucous membrane</u> and <u>skin</u> <u>burns</u>, <u>acute lung injury</u>, and <u>chemical pneumonitis</u>. <u>Asphyxiants</u> primarily cause systemic and tissue <u>hypoxia</u> by displacing oxygen from inhaled air (e.g., carbon dioxide, <u>methane</u>) or by disrupting oxygen transport and/or oxidative metabolism (e.g., <u>carbon monoxide</u>, <u>phosphine</u>, <u>nitric oxide</u>). Exposure to <u>asphyxiants</u> can lead to <u>hypoxemia</u>, <u>metabolic acidosis</u>, and cardiovascular collapse. Symptoms and signs of both irritant and <u>asphyxiant</u> <u>poisoning</u> may be seen following exposure to certain substances, such as <u>hydrogen sulfide</u> or <u>nitrogen oxides</u>. Management is based primarily on the clinical manifestations. The use of <u>personal protective equipment</u> (<u>PPE</u>) and thorough decontamination is essential to prevent further patient and medical staff exposure. Resuscitation and <u>supportive care</u> are the mainstays of treatment. In some cases, substance-specific measures (e.g., <u>antidotes</u>) are indicated.




This article outlines common sources of irritant and <u>asphyxiant</u> <u>poisoning</u>. Other hazardous chemicals are discussed in “<u>Smoke inhalation injury</u>,” “<u>Organic solvent toxicity</u>,” “<u>Hydrocarbon toxicity</u>,” “<u>Carbon monoxide toxicity</u>,” “<u>Carbon dioxide poisoning</u>,” “<u>Cyanide toxicity</u>,” “<u>Caustic agents</u>,” and “<u>Cholinergic poisoning</u>.”

---

## Ammonia

This section provides an overview of environmental <u>ammonia</u> exposure. See “<u>Hyperammonemia</u>” for <u>endogenous</u> causes.




* Characteristics [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[3]](/library/woWhVm0)

* <u>Highly water-soluble irritant</u>

* Colorless

* Pungent odor

* Sources of exposure [[3]](/library/woWhVm0)

* Accidents during manufacturing or transportation

* Use of cleaning products, fertilizers, or refrigerants that contain <u>ammonia</u> (e.g., anhydrous ammonia)

* Pathophysiology: <u>exothermic</u> reaction upon contact with moist surfaces (e.g., <u>mucous membranes</u>) → thermal and caustic injury to <u>skin</u>, eyes, <u>oral cavity</u>, and/or respiratory tract [[3]](/library/woWhVm0)

* Clinical features [[3]](/library/woWhVm0)[[4]](/library/avcQAV0)

* Respiratory tract: throat irritation, <u>cough</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>rhinorrhea</u>, chest tightness  [[3]](/library/woWhVm0)

* Ocular: <u>conjunctival</u> irritation, corneal damage

* <u>Dermal</u>: <u>pain</u>, irritation, <u>necrosis</u>, <u>blistering</u>, deep <u>burns</u>, <u>frostbite</u>

* Gastrointestinal : corrosive injury to mouth, throat, <u>esophagus</u>, and/or <u>stomach</u>

* Initial management: Follow the <u>approach to asphyxiant and irritant exposure</u>.

* Substance-specific diagnostics [[4]](/library/avcQAV0)

* <u>CXR</u>: may show <u>pulmonary edema</u>

* No confirmatory study is available.

* Substance-specific management

* For ingestional exposure: [[4]](/library/avcQAV0)

* Avoid <u>gastrointestinal decontamination</u>.

* Have the patient drink 4–8 oz of water.

* Consider GI consult for <u>EGD</u>.

* For severe <u>inhalational injury</u>: consider pulmonary consult for <u>bronchoscopy</u>.

* No specific <u>antidote</u> is available.

* Complications [[4]](/library/avcQAV0)

* Respiratory: chronic <u>lung</u> disease (e.g., <u>asthma</u>, <u>pulmonary fibrosis</u>), <u>respiratory failure</u>

* <u>Dermal</u>: severe <u>burns</u>, deep <u>ulcerations</u>, chronic dermatitis

* Ocular: <u>cataracts</u>, <u>glaucoma</u>, blindness

* Gastrointestinal: <u>GI perforation</u>, strictures





> [!TIP]
> <u>Ammonia</u> exposure typically manifests with the immediate onset of <u>superficial</u> <u>mucosa</u> symptoms (e.g., <u>lacrimation</u>, <u>rhinorrhea</u>, burning sensation). Severe exposure may lead to <u>airway obstruction</u> and <u>pulmonary edema</u>. [[3]](/library/woWhVm0)

## Nitrogen oxides

This section provides an overview of <u>nitric oxide</u> and <u>nitrogen dioxide poisoning</u>; <u>nitrous oxide</u> is used as an <u>anesthetic</u> and has a different toxicity profile.




* Definition: a group of gaseous oxides that contain nitrogen; includes <u>nitric oxide</u> and nitrogen dioxide [[10]](/library/mKWVSm0)

* Characteristics [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/mKWVSm0)

* <u>Nitric oxide</u>: <u>chemical asphyxiant</u>; colorless and odorless at room temperature

* Nitrogen dioxide: <u>poorly water-soluble irritant</u>; red-brown at room temperature, sharp odor  [[10]](/library/mKWVSm0)

* Sources of exposure

* Industrial: engine exhausts, electric arc welding

* <u>Decomposition</u> of silage (silo filler's disease)  [[11]](/library/MKWMSm0)

* Pathophysiology [[10]](/library/mKWVSm0)

* <u>Nitric oxide</u>

* Potent inducer of <u>methemoglobinemia</u>

* Unstable in air and undergoes oxidation to nitrogen dioxide

* Nitrogen dioxide: comes into contact with water in the respiratory tract → production of nitric and nitrous acids and formation of toxic <u>free radicals</u> → irritation and/or burning of <u>distal</u> <u>bronchi</u> and alveolar damage

* Clinical features: Immediate symptoms (e.g., <u>cough</u>, <u>nausea</u>) may be followed by a symptom-free period (3–30 hours) before the onset of <u>chemical pneumonitis</u>.

* Respiratory: <u>cough</u>, <u>pulmonary edema</u>, <u>hypoxemia</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>bronchospasm</u>

* <u>Dermal</u>: chemical <u>burns</u>

* Ocular: irritation and <u>ocular burns</u>

* Gastrointestinal: <u>nausea</u>, abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Initial management: Follow the <u>approach to asphyxiant and irritant exposure</u>.

* Substance-specific diagnostics [[10]](/library/mKWVSm0)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: ↑ <u>methemoglobin</u> levels for <u>nitric oxide</u> exposure

* Confirmatory study: measure urine nitrogen oxide metabolites

* Substance-specific management [[10]](/library/mKWVSm0)

* Consider <u>methylene blue</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE for patients with <u>signs of hypoxia</u> (other than <u>cyanosis</u>) or <u>methemoglobin</u> levels > 30%.

* If the patient continues to worsen, consider <u>exchange transfusion</u> with specialist guidance.

* No specific <u>antidote</u> is available.

* Complications

* <u>Bronchiolitis obliterans</u>

* <u>ARDS</u>
